justification_text:
My point estimates across all three horizons reflect a relatively stable baseline with only modest drift. At the one-day horizon, I anchored close to the most recent observed price or level, assuming mean-reverting dynamics dominate over very short windows and that no immediate catalysts were likely to produce a sharp move. The one-week estimate drifted only slightly higher, reflecting a mild underlying trend or drift assumption while still being dominated by recent momentum. At one month, I allowed for a bit more upward drift, consistent with a slow-moving fundamental or trend component, but the magnitude of change remained small relative to the uncertainty bands, suggesting I believed the asset or variable was broadly range-bound over this period.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated primarily to historical volatility at each respective horizon. For one day, the relatively tight 19-point range reflects that short-horizon realized volatility tends to be modest in absolute terms, and autocorrelation in returns or levels over very short windows limits how far things typically move. As the horizon extends to one week and one month, the intervals widen substantially — from roughly 34 points at one week to 67 points at one month — following a rough square-root-of-time scaling logic. Additional uncertainty at longer horizons also stems from the possibility of regime changes, macroeconomic surprises, or shifts in sentiment that compound over time and are genuinely unknowable at the time of the forecast.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals include sudden policy announcements, geopolitical shocks, or unexpected data releases that move markets discontinuously rather than through gradual drift. At the one-month horizon in particular, the tails are fatter in practice than a normal distribution would suggest, meaning black-swan-style events — a financial contagion scare, a major central bank surprise, or a geopolitical escalation — could easily place realized outcomes well below 265 or above 332. Liquidity conditions and correlated asset dislocations could also amplify moves beyond what historical volatility alone would imply, especially in stressed market environments where normal mean-reversion breaks down.

Finally, I should acknowledge model uncertainty as a source of risk to the intervals themselves. If the underlying data-generating process has shifted — for instance, if there is a structural break in trend or volatility regime — then my intervals could be systematically miscalibrated rather than just unlucky. The one-month window is especially exposed to this risk, since a month is long enough for a new regime to become entrenched but short enough that I may not have incorporated early signals of the shift into my forecast at the time it was made.
